chapter: Changing styles, the road and nightlife
title: Nostalgia craze and his call-in jazz radio shows
summary: Saunders sees a nostalgic return to older players and recalls radio appearances on jazz stations where listeners called in.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: How the music business changed: hype, youth and lost apprenticeship

blocks.x: Do you ever see any possibility of this changing?

I don't know. People -- you can't hardly predict what people will do. But one of the fortunate things that has happened in the last few years is the nostalgic craze. Everybody's going back, and then you find these guys, they're digging them up out of the woodwork, and these guys are coming back and they're really playing and the people are recognizing. Because we've gone to this period of forced entertainment, I would say. The promoters and things force you to buy what they want you to buy, because it's just so much of it on the market.

Right, brainwashing is the phrase. Because -- and then, say, give you what they want you to have. But people still -- I did some radio shows here on a couple of the jazz stations. And the people that called me, it was amazing the people that are listening.
I heard you on Count B.J.
Right, right, it was very -- and then he opened the phone calls, they had phone calls. And I talked to people -- I mean, man, I wouldn't dream of listening.

Rav Martury was one, he called. And Warren Kime and these kind of guys. I mean, just jazz players and besides the musicians, then the jazz public. And all the musicians. And I got so many compliments -- not compliments, but so many people said they heard me, that didn't even call. And in a short period of time, that phone was jumping. Yeah.
You're sort of the father figure in Chicago music.
